title: Distributed computing scope and evidence
summary: Build a systems-first study loop: scale, hardware limits, failure, coordination, and project evidence.
objectives: Name the first six lecture themes
Separate compute, communication, coordination, and failure questions
Design a reproducible distributed experiment record

sections.title: Lecture core · why distributed systems
sections.body: The course starts from a systems constraint: data grows faster than one machine can comfortably store, move, or process, while hardware and networks can fail. A useful experiment records scale, partitioning, communication, coordination, and failure assumptions instead of reporting one opaque runtime.

sourceLens.whyExaminable: The overview is examinable because it supplies the vocabulary used to interpret every later algorithm and project result.

sections.title: Project evidence, not project folklore
sections.body: The supplied overview lists three group projects and identifies the first two themes: consistency testing with a distributed database and machine learning with Apache Spark. Dates and later lecture details remain pending until their official sources are supplied.

sourceLens.whyExaminable: Project work becomes learnable when the claim, measurement, system setting, and failure assumption are explicit.

examples.title: Distributed experiment record
steps: State the input size and worker count.
Record the partitioning and communication pattern.
Name the failure or consistency assumption.
Report throughput, latency, shuffle, coordination, and recovery evidence.
examples.answer: A systems claim is credible only when the environment and observed costs are part of the result.

contrastDrills.prompt: Two runs perform the same arithmetic, but one moves ten times more data between workers. Which cost changed?
contrastDrills.explanation: The arithmetic is unchanged; data movement and message transfer changed the communication cost.
contrastDrills.misconception: Name the ordering, time, or communication boundary before choosing.

math.explanation: A distributed experiment should report more than compute time. Network transfer and coordination barriers can dominate as the worker count grows, so record them separately whenever the system exposes them.
math.name: Distributed-job cost decomposition
math.purpose: Use it to measure useful work separately from network movement and coordination overhead.

math.explanation: Use this as a diagnostic decomposition for a distributed experiment. It is a study model, not a universal runtime identity: storage, skew, failures, and serialization may add further terms.

symbols.meaning: time spent moving data or messages
time spent waiting for synchronization or scheduling

math.name: Distributed-job cost decomposition
math.purpose: Use it to diagnose whether compute, network movement, or coordination dominates a distributed workload.
math.caveat: The lecture overview motivates these dimensions but does not present this exact equation.

criticalQuestions.prompt: Why is one average runtime insufficient evidence for a distributed-system claim?
criticalQuestions.angle: Separate useful work from communication, coordination, partition skew, and failure recovery.
criticalQuestions.modelAnswer: The average hides the conditions that produce the cost. Record worker count, partitioning, network movement, coordination, and failure behavior before comparing designs.

criticalQuestions.prompt: When could adding workers increase total runtime?
criticalQuestions.angle: Look for communication and coordination terms that grow faster than useful computation falls.
criticalQuestions.modelAnswer: If network, synchronization, serialization, or skew dominates, the added workers can increase overhead instead of improving throughput.
